lead: This unit explains why an amplifier's gain falls at low and high frequencies, and how power amplifiers deliver large signals efficiently. After it you can find lower and upper cut-off frequencies, use Miller's theorem and gain-bandwidth product, choose a wideband or tuned stage, and design class A, B, AB, C and D output stages with efficiency, distortion and heat-sink calculations.
about: This unit follows the gain of an amplifier from DC to its high-frequency limit and then turns to stages that deliver power. Chapter 3.1 finds the lower cut-off from coupling and bypass capacitors. Chapter 3.2 uses the hybrid-pi model and Miller effect to find the upper cut-off. Chapter 3.3 connects gain and bandwidth through transition frequency. Chapter 3.4 compares wideband and tuned stages. Chapters 3.5 to 3.7 cover class A, B, AB, C and D power amplifiers, efficiency and crossover distortion. Chapter 3.8 closes with total harmonic distortion and heat-sink design.

chapters.idea: An amplifier's gain falls at low frequency because coupling and bypass capacitors stop acting as short circuits; the lower cut-off fL is where gain is 0.707 of midband.
chapters.depth: Explain the RC high-pass idea for each capacitor: input coupling, output coupling and emitter bypass in a BJT stage, and source or gate capacitors in a FET stage. Define fL = 1/(2πRC) and show that the largest individual fL dominates. Cover the Bode magnitude plot, midband gain, the -3 dB point and the start of bandwidth. Some syllabi call this the low-frequency response or f1. Include the effect of the emitter bypass capacitor on emitter resistance. Keep hybrid-pi high-frequency detail for Chapter 3.2.

figure.aria: Two high-pass gain curves; each curve is 3 dB below the 40 dB midband level at its lower cut-off, 50 Hz and 200 Hz.

chapters.example: A CE amplifier has input resistance 10 kΩ, input coupling capacitor 1 µF, output resistance 50 kΩ and output coupling capacitor 0.1 µF. Midband gain is 100. Find each lower cut-off, the overall fL, and the gain at 10 Hz. Solution: f1 = 1/(2π×10^4×10^-6) = 15.9 Hz. f2 = 1/(2π×50×10^3×0.1×10^-6) = 31.8 Hz. The larger value sets fL ≈ 31.8 Hz. At 10 Hz, f/fL = 0.314, gain = 100×0.314/√(1+0.314²) = 30.0.
chapters.trap: Using the smallest individual cut-off as fL, or saying gain at fL is full midband gain; at fL it is 0.707 of midband.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: RC coupling, CE amplifier, input and output resistance.
chapters.leave: Hybrid-pi high-frequency model and Miller effect to Chapter 3.2; multistage bandwidth to Chapter 3.4.

chapters.idea: At high frequency, internal capacitances and the Miller effect reduce gain; the upper cut-off fH is where gain falls to 0.707 of midband.
chapters.depth: Introduce the hybrid-pi model for the BJT: rπ, gm, Cπ and Cμ; and the FET model with Cgs and Cgd. Derive Miller input capacitance C_M = Cμ(1+|A_v|) and output capacitance C_out ≈ Cμ(1+1/|A_v|). Show fH = 1/(2πR_eqC_eq). Cover input and output time constants, dominant pole, and why a CE stage has a poor high-frequency response. Some syllabi call Cπ the diffusion capacitance and Cμ the transition capacitance. Mention the Miller effect in FETs as Cgd(1+|A_v|). Keep gain-bandwidth product for Chapter 3.3.

figure.aria: The feedback capacitor Cμ from output to input appears at the input as a much larger Miller capacitance Cμ(1+A), shunting the input node.

chapters.example: A CE stage has |A_v| = 100, Cμ = 2 pF, Cπ = 10 pF, and source resistance 1 kΩ; take rπ large enough to ignore. Find the Miller input capacitance, total input capacitance, output Miller capacitance, and fH. Solution: C_M = 2 pF×(1+100) = 202 pF. Total input C = 202+10 = 212 pF. fH = 1/(2π×1000×212×10^-12) = 750 kHz. Output Miller C = 2 pF×(1+1/100) ≈ 2.02 pF.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the (1+|A|) multiplication, or adding Cπ to Cμ before multiplying; the Miller capacitance is Cμ(1+|A|), not Cμ|A|.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 hybrid-pi model; Chapter 3.1 midband gain and RC time constant.
chapters.leave: Gain-bandwidth product to Chapter 3.3; feedback bandwidth improvement to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: For a dominant-pole amplifier, gain × bandwidth is constant; transition frequency fT is the frequency where open-loop gain falls to 1.
chapters.depth: Define GBW = A0 × f_p = fT for a single-pole op-amp or amplifier. Show open-loop gain A(f) = A0/√(1+(f/f_p)²), and above f_p A(f) ≈ fT/f. Define transition frequency fT where |A| = 1. Explain closed-loop bandwidth = fT/closed-loop gain for a non-inverting amplifier. Mention that GBW is a figure of merit; some syllabi call fT the unity-gain frequency or cut-off frequency. Include the relation to slew rate only as a forward pointer to Unit 5.

figure.aria: A plot of open-loop gain against frequency. The gain falls as 1/f and reaches 1 at 1 MHz, so the gain-bandwidth product is 10^6.

chapters.example: An op-amp has low-frequency gain A0 = 200,000 and transition frequency fT = 2 MHz. Find the dominant pole frequency and the closed-loop bandwidth at a gain of 20. Solution: f_p = fT/A0 = 2×10^6/2×10^5 = 10 Hz. GBW = fT = 2 MHz. Closed-loop BW = GBW/20 = 100 kHz.
chapters.trap: Using fT as the closed-loop bandwidth at every gain; the closed-loop bandwidth is fT divided by the closed-loop gain.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.2 upper cut-off; Unit 6 op-amp ideal model.
chapters.leave: Slew rate, compensation and op-amp internals to Unit 5; feedback topologies to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Wideband amplifiers trade gain for bandwidth using cascode or CC-CE stages, while tuned amplifiers trade bandwidth for gain at a chosen centre frequency.
chapters.depth: Cover widebanding techniques: cascode (CE-CB), CC-CE cascade, CD-CS cascade, Darlington pair, and emitter peaking. Explain how cascode reduces the Miller effect. For tuned amplifiers, define centre frequency f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)), quality factor Q, bandwidth BW = f0/Q, and voltage gain at resonance. Mention single tuned and double tuned; some syllabi call this an RF tuned amplifier. Keep circuit bias in Unit 2. Show a comparison of gain, bandwidth and Miller capacitance.

figure.aria: A tree splits amplifiers into wideband techniques (cascode, CC-CE, Darlington) and tuned LC amplifiers (single and double tuned).

chapters.example: A tuned amplifier has L = 100 µH, C = 100 pF and coil resistance R = 10 Ω. Find f0, Q and bandwidth. Solution: f0 = 1/(2π√(100×10^-6×100×10^-12)) = 1.59 MHz. Q = (1/R)√(L/C) = (1/10)√(100×10^-6/100×10^-12) = 100. BW = f0/Q = 15.9 kHz.
chapters.trap: Using Q = f0/BW to find Q from the components; Q must first come from R, L and C, then BW = f0/Q.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.2 Miller effect; Unit 2 cascode and Darlington connections.
chapters.leave: Feedback broadbanding to Unit 4; oscillator LC tanks to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Power amplifier classes differ in conduction angle; class A conducts all the time, class B half the time, and efficiency rises as conduction angle falls.
chapters.depth: Define conduction angle, quiescent power, output power and conversion efficiency η = P_out/P_DC. Cover class A in series-fed and transformer-coupled forms, class B, class AB and class C briefly; class D is in Chapter 3.7. Derive maximum efficiency: class A series-fed 25%, transformer-coupled 50%, class B 78.5%, class C can approach 90% with a tuned load. Include load line and signal swing. Some syllabi call conversion efficiency the collector efficiency. Solve numerical problems.

figure.title: Power amplifier classes
figure.aria: A comparison table: class A conducts for 360° with low distortion and about 25% maximum efficiency; class B for 180° with crossover distortion and 78% efficiency; class AB in between; class C has a short angle and high efficiency; class D uses PWM switching.

chapters.example: A series-fed class A amplifier has Vcc = 12 V, Rc = 1 kΩ and is biased at midpoint (Vce = 6 V, Ic = 6 mA). Find DC input power, maximum AC output power and efficiency. Solution: P_DC = 12 V×6 mA = 72 mW. Peak output voltage = 6 V, peak current = 6 mA. P_out(max) = (6×6 mA)/2 = 18 mW. η = 18/72 = 25%.
chapters.trap: Using P_out = V_peak×I_peak without the factor 1/2, or using Vcc×Ic as AC power and getting 100%.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 load line and CE amplifier; Chapter 3.1 gain.
chapters.leave: Push-pull operation and crossover distortion to Chapter 3.6; class C and D to Chapter 3.7.

chapters.idea: A push-pull class B stage uses two transistors for opposite half-cycles; class AB biases them slightly on to remove the crossover dead zone.
chapters.depth: Explain transformer-coupled and transformerless (OTL) push-pull. For class B, derive P_out(max) = Vcc²/(2RL), P_DC = 2Vcc²/(πRL), η = π/4 = 78.5%. Compare with class A push-pull. For class AB, show bias diodes or a VBE multiplier and small quiescent current. Define crossover distortion as the flat spot near zero caused by the 0.7 V base-emitter drop; class AB removes it at the cost of some quiescent power. Include complementary symmetry and quasi-complementary output. Some syllabi call this push-pull class B/AB.

figure.aria: Push-pull stage: the phase splitter drives an NPN for positive half-cycles and a PNP for negative half-cycles; near zero both are off, giving a dead zone and crossover distortion.

chapters.example: A complementary class B push-pull amplifier has ±12 V supplies and an 8 Ω load. Find maximum output power, DC input power and efficiency. Solution: V_peak = 12 V. P_out = Vcc²/(2RL) = 144/16 = 9 W. P_DC = 2Vcc²/(πRL) = 288/25.13 = 11.46 W. η = 9/11.46 = 78.5%.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that both supplies deliver current, so P_DC is 2Vcc²/(πRL), not Vcc²/(πRL); also using rms 12 V instead of peak.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.5 class A and B efficiency; Unit 2 complementary emitter follower.
chapters.leave: Class C and D to Chapter 3.7; heat-sink design to Chapter 3.8.

chapters.idea: Class C conducts for less than half a cycle and uses a tuned load; class D switches transistors on and off and uses PWM, giving high efficiency.
chapters.depth: Class C: conduction angle less than 180°, tuned LC load restores the sine wave, efficiency high but distortion high; used in RF transmitters. Class D: comparator makes PWM, switching pair, LC low-pass filter; ideal efficiency 100%, practical 85-95%. Explain why class D is used in audio and motor drives. Mention class E and class F only as names. Some syllabi call class D a switching amplifier. Keep heat sinking to Chapter 3.8.

figure.aria: Class D: an audio signal and a triangle carrier drive a comparator, whose PWM output switches MOSFETs; the LC filter removes the carrier and leaves the audio at the load.

chapters.example: A class D audio amplifier delivers 20 W to a load. The switching MOSFETs dissipate 1 W and the LC filter dissipates 0.5 W. Find the efficiency. Solution: P_loss = 1+0.5 = 1.5 W. P_DC = 20+1.5 = 21.5 W. η = 20/21.5 = 93.0%.
chapters.trap: Assuming class D is 100% efficient and ignoring switching and filter losses; also confusing class C's tuned load with class D's LC filter.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.6 push-pull switching of two devices; Unit 1 diode and switch basics.
chapters.leave: Harmonic distortion and heat sinks to Chapter 3.8; PWM generation with 555 timer to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: Harmonic distortion measures unwanted multiples of the signal, and a heat sink keeps the transistor junction below its maximum temperature.
chapters.depth: Define harmonics and THD = √(V2²+V3²+…)/V1 for voltages, and THD in dB. Explain the Fourier idea without heavy maths. Cover thermal resistance Rθ for junction-to-case, case-to-sink and sink-to-ambient, power dissipation, and Tj = Ta + P_D(Rθ_jc+Rθ_cs+Rθ_sa). Show heat-sink selection. Mention derating and thermal runaway briefly. Some syllabi call THD total harmonic distortion. Keep distortion reduction by feedback in Unit 4.

figure.aria: Layers from the transistor junction to the case, heat sink and ambient; heat flows down this path and each layer adds thermal resistance.

chapters.example: A 1 kHz amplifier output has fundamental 10 V rms, second harmonic 0.5 V rms and third harmonic 0.3 V rms. The transistor dissipates 8 W. Rθ_jc = 2 °C/W, Rθ_cs = 1 °C/W, ambient 40 °C, maximum junction 150 °C. Find THD and the maximum allowed heat-sink thermal resistance. Solution: THD = √(0.5²+0.3²)/10 = 0.583/10 = 5.83%. Rθ_sa ≤ (150-40)/8 - (2+1) = 13.75-3 = 10.75 °C/W.
chapters.trap: Adding harmonic voltages directly instead of taking the square root of squares; forgetting Rθ_cs in the thermal path.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.6 and 3.7 power stages; Unit 2 transistor power limits.
chapters.leave: Negative feedback to reduce distortion to Unit 4; thermal design of IC regulators to Unit 1.

links: fL and fH together form the bandwidth
Miller capacitance sets fH; GBW links gain and bandwidth
GBW sets the limit for wideband stages
wideband stages drive power output stages
class A leads to class B push-pull
class B/AB crossover leads to class C and D switching
switching and power losses need THD and heat sinks
